mcqs.question: Which is the strongest operational definition of "scalable"?
options: The system runs on cloud infrastructure with auto-scaling enabled
Adding capacity increases what the system can handle, roughly linearly, with no hidden ceiling
The system has a load balancer in front of multiple servers
The system has never gone down in production
mcqs.explanation: A useful definition of scalable is falsifiable — it makes a checkable claim about how capacity relates to added resources. Running on the cloud, having a load balancer, or having a clean uptime record don't actually establish that adding nodes proportionally increases capacity.

mcqs.question: A design handles 10k QPS on 10 nodes, but the database saturates at the equivalent of 40 nodes' worth of load. If the target is 100k QPS, what does this tell you?
options: The design doesn't reach the target as-is — the database becomes the bottleneck well before 100 nodes get you there
The design already meets the target since app nodes can simply be added indefinitely
The target is irrelevant once you've shown the app tier scales linearly
Sharding will never be necessary since the app tier is stateless
mcqs.explanation: Testing the design against the actual target reveals the database saturates around 40k QPS, well short of the 100k target, so the app tier's linear scaling doesn't carry the whole system there. The app tier's statelessness doesn't rescue a saturated single database.

mcqs.question: Why can a design be highly scalable for reads but hit a scaling wall on writes at a much lower number?
options: Reads and writes always scale identically in any well-designed system
Writes are inherently impossible to scale under any circumstances
Many replicas of the same data can serve many readers in parallel, but a single logical write stream doesn't automatically parallelize the same way
Reads require more total compute resources than writes in every system
mcqs.explanation: Read scaling benefits from duplicating the same data across replicas so many readers can be served in parallel; writes have to eventually land somewhere consistent, so simply adding nodes doesn't parallelize a single write stream the same way. Writes can be scaled (via sharding), just not by the same mechanism as reads.

mcqs.question: A candidate says "this design is scalable" without naming an axis or a ceiling. What's missing?
options: Nothing — the word "scalable" is self-explanatory and sufficient
A specific brand name of cloud provider being used
A discussion of the system's total server count only
A stated axis (users, data, requests) and the point at which the design stops scaling linearly
mcqs.explanation: "Scalable" without an axis and a ceiling is an unexamined compliment, not an engineering claim — pairing it with a number and a dimension is what makes it checkable. Neither the cloud vendor nor raw server count captures what's actually being asked.
